claim: Boundary cap (BC) cells form transient aggregates during embryogenesis at the central/peripheral nervous system (CNS/PNS) interface, at the levels of dorsal entry and ventral exit points of all cranial and spinal nerves.
source: Boundary cap (BC) cells form transient aggregates during embryogenesis at the central/peripheral nervous system (CNS/PNS) interface, at the levels of dorsal entry and ventral exit points of all cranial and spinal nerves.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about BC cell location and timing, supported by the citation context of the manuscript.

claim: Most BC cells express the genes Egr2 (also known as Krox20) and/or Prss56 that have been used as molecular markers in functional and tracing studies.
source: Most BC cells express the genes Egr2 (also known as Krox20) and/or Prss56 that have been used as molecular markers in functional and tracing studies (Coulpier et al., 2009; Niederländer and Lumsden, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that established these markers.

claim: Fate mapping experiments using a murine Prss56Cre allele have revealed that Prss56-positive BC cell derivatives migrate between embryonic day (E) 11.5 and E13.5 along nerve roots into dorsal root ganglia (DRGs), where they give rise to Schwann cells (SCs) and a subpopulation of sensory neurons.
source: Fate mapping experiments using a murine Prss56Cre allele have recently revealed that Prss56-positive BC cell derivatives migrate between embryonic day (E) 11.5 and E13.5 along nerve roots into dorsal root ganglia (DRGs), where they give rise to Schwann cells (SCs) and a subpopulation of sensory neurons, and along spinal nerves to reach the skin, where they differentiate into SCs, terminal glia, and melanocytes (Gresset et al., 2015; Radomska et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: Prss56-positive BC cell derivatives migrate along spinal nerves to reach the skin, where they differentiate into SCs, terminal glia, and melanocytes.
source: Fate mapping experiments using a murine Prss56Cre allele have recently revealed that Prss56-positive BC cell derivatives migrate between embryonic day (E) 11.5 and E13.5 along nerve roots into dorsal root ganglia (DRGs), where they give rise to Schwann cells (SCs) and a subpopulation of sensory neurons, and along spinal nerves to reach the skin, where they differentiate into SCs, terminal glia, and melanocytes (Gresset et al., 2015; Radomska et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives migrate along spinal nerves to reach the skin.
source: Here, we show that Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives migrate, during the same time period, along spinal nerves to reach the skin.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the current study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives detach from nerves in the skin.
source: In the skin, most of them detach from nerves, integrate the vascular plexus, and provide the major source of MCs to the adult skin vasculature.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives integrate the vascular plexus in the skin.
source: In the skin, most of them detach from nerves, integrate the vascular plexus, and provide the major source of MCs to the adult skin vasculature.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Egr2-positive BC cell derivatives provide the major source of mural cells to the adult skin vasculature.
source: In the skin, most of them detach from nerves, integrate the vascular plexus, and provide the major source of MCs to the adult skin vasculature.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantification data showing that traced cells represent 68% and 66% of NG2-positive MCs at E15.5 and P1, respectively.

claim: Numerous Tom-positive cells were found in the dorsal and ventral roots at E11.5.
source: As previously reported, we found numerous Tom-positive cells in the dorsal and ventral roots at E11.5 (Figure 1A), as well as in the DRGs at E12.5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observation in Figure 1A showing Tom-positive cells in roots.

claim: Traced cells were observed in the DRGs at E12.5.
source: As previously reported, we found numerous Tom-positive cells in the dorsal and ventral roots at E11.5 (Figure 1A), as well as in the DRGs at E12.5 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observation in Figure 1B.

claim: Traced cells were observed in the proximal spinal nerve segments at E11.5.
source: In addition, traced cells were observed in the proximal spinal nerve segments at E11.5 (Figure 1A and D), in the intermediate segments of dorsal and ventral rami at E12.5 (Figure 1B and E) and E13.5 (Figure 1C), and finally at dorsal and ventral skin nerve terminals from E13.5 (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1A and D.

claim: Traced cells were observed in the intermediate segments of dorsal and ventral rami at E12.5 and E13.5.
source: In addition, traced cells were observed in the proximal spinal nerve segments at E11.5 (Figure 1A and D), in the intermediate segments of dorsal and ventral rami at E12.5 (Figure 1B and E) and E13.5 (Figure 1C), and finally at dorsal and ventral skin nerve terminals from E13.5 (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy images in Figures 1B, E, and C.

claim: Traced cells were observed at dorsal and ventral skin nerve terminals from E13.5.
source: In addition, traced cells were observed in the proximal spinal nerve segments at E11.5 (Figure 1A and D), in the intermediate segments of dorsal and ventral rami at E12.5 (Figure 1B and E) and E13.5 (Figure 1C), and finally at dorsal and ventral skin nerve terminals from E13.5 (Figure 1C and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy images in Figure 1C and F.

claim: The dynamic time-course of proximo-distal distributions of traced cells strongly suggests a migration of derivatives of Egr2-positive BC cells along nerves.
source: This dynamic time-course of proximo-distal distributions strongly suggests a migration of derivatives of Egr2-positive BC cells along nerves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal and spatial distribution patterns observed in the data.

claim: Some traced cells were not in contact with nerves, near the ventral roots at E11.5–12.5.
source: We also noticed that some of the traced cells were not in contact with nerves, near the ventral roots at E11.5–12.5 (Figure 1A and B, arrows) and later in the skin (Figure 1C and F, arrows).
evidence: This observation is directly shown in Figure 1A and B with arrows indicating detached cells.

claim: Some traced cells were not in contact with nerves in the skin.
source: We also noticed that some of the traced cells were not in contact with nerves, near the ventral roots at E11.5–12.5 (Figure 1A and B, arrows) and later in the skin (Figure 1C and F, arrows).
evidence: This observation is directly shown in Figure 1C and F with arrows indicating detached cells.

claim: Egr2 expression was not detected in the skin at E12.5 by in situ hybridization on whole embryos.
source: To ensure that all traced cells originate from Krox-20-positive BC cells, i.e., that Tom expression does not result from de novo activation of Egr2 in other cells populations, we searched for Egr2 expression at E12.5 by in situ hybridization on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), RT-PCR analysis of total RNA extracted skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and RNAscope on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–J). These experiments did not reveal the presence of Egr2 mRNA apart from BC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Egr2 expression was not detected in the skin at E12.5 by RT-PCR analysis of total RNA extracted from skin.
source: To ensure that all traced cells originate from Krox-20-positive BC cells, i.e., that Tom expression does not result from de novo activation of Egr2 in other cells populations, we searched for Egr2 expression at E12.5 by in situ hybridization on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), RT-PCR analysis of total RNA extracted skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and RNAscope on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–J). These experiments did not reveal the presence of Egr2 mRNA apart from BC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Egr2 expression was not detected in the skin at E12.5 by RNAscope on whole embryos.
source: To ensure that all traced cells originate from Krox-20-positive BC cells, i.e., that Tom expression does not result from de novo activation of Egr2 in other cells populations, we searched for Egr2 expression at E12.5 by in situ hybridization on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), RT-PCR analysis of total RNA extracted skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and RNAscope on whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–J). These experiments did not reveal the presence of Egr2 mRNA apart from BC cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–J.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of Tom-positive skin cells in E12.5 Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos did not reveal any expression of Cre.
source: Furthermore, single-cell transcriptomic analysis of Tom-positive skin cells in E12.5 Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos did not reveal any expression of Cre (see below).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis.

claim: There is an absence of de novo Egr2 expression in traced cells outside of the BC.
source: Together these data indicate the absence of de novo Egr2 expression in traced cells outside of the BC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence (in situ hybridization, RT-PCR, RNAscope, and scRNA-seq).

claim: Derivatives from Egr2-expressing BC cells migrate along spinal nerves into the skin.
source: In conclusion, these analyses establish that derivatives from Egr2-expressing BC cells migrate along spinal nerves into the skin, and that some of them detach from the nerves during their journey.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the temporal and spatial distribution data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Some derivatives from Egr2-expressing BC cells detach from the nerves during their journey to the skin.
source: In conclusion, these analyses establish that derivatives from Egr2-expressing BC cells migrate along spinal nerves into the skin, and that some of them detach from the nerves during their journey.
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by observations of cells not in contact with nerves shown in Figure 1.

claim: 89.9% (SD 6.5%) of traced cells were in contact with nerves at E12.5.
source: Whereas 89.9% (SD 6.5%) of the traced cells were in contact with nerves at E12.5, this proportion rapidly diminished to reach 9.4% (SD 6.3%) at E15.5 (Figure 1G–J and M).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1M.

claim: The proportion of traced cells in contact with nerves rapidly diminished to reach 9.4% (SD 6.3%) at E15.5.
source: Whereas 89.9% (SD 6.5%) of the traced cells were in contact with nerves at E12.5, this proportion rapidly diminished to reach 9.4% (SD 6.3%) at E15.5 (Figure 1G–J and M).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Traced cells were found in contact with blood vessels in increasing proportions, from 10.1% (SD 6.4%) at E12.5 up to 90.6% (SD 6.3%) at E15.5.
source: Conversely, traced cells were found in contact with blood vessels in increasing proportions, from 10.1% (SD 6.4%) at E12.5 up to 90.6% (SD 6.3%) at E15.5 (Figure 1G–J and L).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from whole-mount immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1M.

claim: Traced cells in contact with capillaries and larger vessels did not express the endothelial marker PECAM.
source: Traced cells in contact with capillaries and larger vessels did not express the endothelial marker PECAM, raising the possibility that they might have acquired an MC identity (Figure 1H–K).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 1H–K by the lack of colocalization between Tom and PECAM.

claim: A few traced cells were observed straddling both nerves and vessels.
source: Finally, a few traced cells were observed straddling both nerves and vessels (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This observation is directly shown in Figure 1K and L.

claim: Most traced cells, after having traveled from the BCs to the skin along nerves, detach from nerves and are recruited within the vascular plexus.
source: Together these data suggest that most traced cells, after having traveled from the BCs to the skin along nerves, detach from nerves and are recruited within the vascular plexus.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the quantitative data showing the shift from nerve-associated to vessel-associated cells over time.

claim: The behavior of Egr2-traced cells dramatically differs from that of derivatives of Prss56-positive BC cells.
source: Their behavior dramatically differs from that of derivatives of Prss56-positive BC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–M and N–P), which migrate along the same nerves over the same time period, but remain associated with nerves in their vast majority (Gresset et al., 2015).
evidence: This comparison is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: Derivatives of Prss56-positive BC cells migrate along the same nerves over the same time period as Egr2-traced cells, but remain associated with nerves in their vast majority.
source: Their behavior dramatically differs from that of derivatives of Prss56-positive BC cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–M and N–P), which migrate along the same nerves over the same time period, but remain associated with nerves in their vast majority (Gresset et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N–P and citation to previous work.

claim: Egr2 inactivation does not affect the association of Egr2-traced derivatives to the vascular plexus.
source: We did not observe any obvious difference in the pattern and number of Tom-positive cells in contact with blood vessels at E14.5, as compared to Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom control embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1K–M and Q–S).
evidence: This observation is supported by comparison of mutant and control embryos shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Egr2 does not play a role in the migration of BC cell derivatives and in their contribution to the vascular plexus.
source: These latter data do not support a role of Egr2 in the migration of BC cell derivatives and in their contribution to the vascular plexus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of phenotype in Egr2 mutants.

claim: At E14.5, traced cells associated with the vascular network showed characteristic morphologies compatible with pericyte or vSMC identities.
source: We found that at E14.5, traced cells associated with the vascular network showed characteristic morphologies compatible with pericyte or vSMC identities, as they covered small capillaries or wrapped around larger vessels, both arteries and veins (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This observation is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Traced cells associated with the vascular network covered small capillaries or wrapped around larger vessels, both arteries and veins.
source: We found that at E14.5, traced cells associated with the vascular network showed characteristic morphologies compatible with pericyte or vSMC identities, as they covered small capillaries or wrapped around larger vessels, both arteries and veins (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This observation is directly shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Traced cells associated with the vascular network expressed several MC markers, such as ABCC9, NG2, PDGFRβ, and smooth muscle actin (SMA).
source: Consistently, these cells expressed several MC markers, such as ABCC9, NG2, PDGFRβ, and smooth muscle actin (SMA) (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunolabeling shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: Traced cells represented 68% (SD 4.6%) of the NG2-positive MCs in E15.5 skin whole-mounts.
source: Quantification studies of traced cells in E15.5 skin whole-mounts and in postnatal day 1 (P1) skin sections revealed that they represented respectively 68% (SD 4.6%) and 66% (SD 8.1%) of the NG2-positive MCs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Traced cells represented 66% (SD 8.1%) of the NG2-positive MCs in postnatal day 1 (P1) skin sections.
source: Quantification studies of traced cells in E15.5 skin whole-mounts and in postnatal day 1 (P1) skin sections revealed that they represented respectively 68% (SD 4.6%) and 66% (SD 8.1%) of the NG2-positive MCs (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Numerous BC cell-derived MCs persist on capillaries, arteries, and veins in newborn and P30 dorsal skin.
source: Whole-mount analysis of newborn and P30 dorsal skin indicated the persistence of numerous BC cell-derived MCs on capillaries, arteries, and veins (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: Derivatives of Egr2-expressing BC cells detach from nerves, adopt mural characteristics, and constitute the major part of the embryonic and newborn MC component in the skin.
source: Overall, these data indicate that, in the skin, derivatives of Egr2-positive BCs detach from nerves, adopt mural characteristics, and constitute the major part of the embryonic and newborn MC component.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the morphological, marker expression, and quantification data presented.

claim: The BC cell-derived MC population is maintained up to P30 at least.
source: Furthermore, this BC cell-derived MC population is maintained up to P30 at least.
evidence: This is supported by the observation of traced MCs at P30 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A majority of Tom-positive cells on ventral roots at E12.5 were positive for both tomato and Sox10 protein.
source: We observed a majority of cells positive for both tomato and the Sox10, protein, but also some nerve-attached Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This observation is shown by immunolabeling in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Some nerve-attached Tom-positive cells on ventral roots at E12.5 were Sox10-negative at the protein level.
source: We observed a majority of cells positive for both tomato and the Sox10, protein, but also some nerve-attached Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This observation is shown by immunolabeling in Figure 3A–C with arrows indicating Sox10-negative cells.

claim: Similar results showing Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells were obtained by RNAscope, combining Tomato and Sox10 probes.
source: Similar results were obtained by RNAscope, combining Tomato and Sox10 probes (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3D–F.

claim: Among nerve-attached Tom-positive cells on skin nerve endings at E12.5, there is a majority of Sox10-positive cells, but also some Sox10-negative cells.
source: This led us to repeat this analysis on skin nerve endings at E12.5 (Figure 3G and H). Similarly, we found among nerve-attached Tom-positive cells a majority of Sox10-positive cells, but also some Sox10-negative cells.
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells were never observed in the dorsal root.
source: An additional argument in favor of an early commitment of some ventral root cells toward a Sox-10-negative fate came from the analysis of the dorsal root (data not shown). In this case, we never observed Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from data not shown in the manuscript.

claim: The absence of Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells in the dorsal root is consistent with the fact that Tom-positive cells do not detach from the dorsal root.
source: This is consistent with the fact that Tom-positive cells do not detach from the dorsal root.
evidence: This is a logical inference connecting the observation to the behavior of cells.

claim: Some tomato-positive cells on ventral roots at E12.5 express Tbx18.
source: To determine whether the presence of Sox10-negative cells would be accompanied by the expression of MP markers on ventral nerve roots, we used RNAscope to assess the expression of Tbx18, Col1a1, and Pdgfra. As triple RNA labeling was technically challenging, we could only perform double labeling, with Tomato and one marker at a time. We found that each of these three markers was co-expressed with Tomato in some cells (Figure 3I–N).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3I–J.

claim: Some tomato-positive cells on ventral roots at E12.5 express Col1a1.
source: To determine whether the presence of Sox10-negative cells would be accompanied by the expression of MP markers on ventral nerve roots, we used RNAscope to assess the expression of Tbx18, Col1a1, and Pdgfra. As triple RNA labeling was technically challenging, we could only perform double labeling, with Tomato and one marker at a time. We found that each of these three markers was co-expressed with Tomato in some cells (Figure 3I–N).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3K–L.

claim: Some tomato-positive cells on ventral roots at E12.5 express Pdgfra.
source: To determine whether the presence of Sox10-negative cells would be accompanied by the expression of MP markers on ventral nerve roots, we used RNAscope to assess the expression of Tbx18, Col1a1, and Pdgfra. As triple RNA labeling was technically challenging, we could only perform double labeling, with Tomato and one marker at a time. We found that each of these three markers was co-expressed with Tomato in some cells (Figure 3I–N).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3M–N.

claim: In the ventral root, there exist cells of mesenchymal identity derived from Egr2-expressing BC cells.
source: In conclusion, in the ventral root, these findings support the existence of cells of mesenchymal identity derived from Egr2-expressing BC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression of mesenchymal markers (Tbx18, Col1a1, Pdgfra) in Tom-positive cells.

claim: Mesenchymal derivatives from Egr2-expressing BC cells migrate along the nerves to reach the skin, then detach and differentiate into MCs.
source: These derivatives further migrate along the nerves to reach the skin, then detach and differentiate into MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating multiple observations about cell migration, detachment, and differentiation.

claim: In the dorsal root, cells that would give rise to MCs do not exist, consistent with the absence of cell detachment from the nerve.
source: In the dorsal root, such cells would not exist, consistent with the absence of cell detachment from the nerve.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of Sox10-negative cells in the dorsal root.

claim: Fate mapping studies performed in chick and mice point to the NC as the population at the origin of dorsal root BC cells.
source: Although fate mapping studies performed in chick and mice point to the NC as the population at the origin of dorsal root BC cells, the situation appears more complex in the case of the ventral root population (George et al., 2007; Kucenas et al., 2008; Yaneza et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fate mapping studies.

claim: The situation regarding the embryonic origin of ventral root BC cells appears more complex than for dorsal root BC cells.
source: Although fate mapping studies performed in chick and mice point to the NC as the population at the origin of dorsal root BC cells, the situation appears more complex in the case of the ventral root population (George et al., 2007; Kucenas et al., 2008; Yaneza et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Only cranial NC was shown to give rise to MCs in the head vasculature.
source: Moreover, only cranial NC was shown to give rise to MCs in the head vasculature and similar potential for thoracic NC was never reported, despite efforts from many teams.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature.

claim: Similar potential for thoracic NC to give rise to MCs was never reported, despite efforts from many teams.
source: Moreover, only cranial NC was shown to give rise to MCs in the head vasculature and similar potential for thoracic NC was never reported, despite efforts from many teams.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Genetic fate mapping using Wnt1Cre, Sox10Cre-Ert2, and Olig2Cre drivers did not identify any traced MCs, either near ventral roots or in the skin.
source: Embryos carrying the different Cre drivers were collected between E12.5 and E14.5 and analyzed by immunohistochemistry. In all cases, we were not able to identify any traced MCs, either near ventral roots or in the skin (Figure 4A–F), in accordance with previous studies that have shown that the NC and neural tube do not contribute to the trunk vasculature (Etchevers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is shown by the absence of traced MCs in Figure 4A–F and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: The NC and neural tube do not contribute to the trunk vasculature.
source: In all cases, we were not able to identify any traced MCs, either near ventral roots or in the skin (Figure 4A–F), in accordance with previous studies that have shown that the NC and neural tube do not contribute to the trunk vasculature (Etchevers et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the current data and citation to previous studies.

claim: A subpopulation of cells derived from BC cells co-express Tbx18 in the ventral root.
source: We noticed that a subpopulation of cells derived from BC cells co-express Tbx18 in the ventral root (Figure 3G–L).
evidence: This is shown by RNAscope data in Figure 3I–J (note: the text references Figure 3G–L but this appears to be a typo based on the figure descriptions).

claim: At E9.5, Tbx18 expression was detected in the vicinity of the neural tube, in a layer of MPs that gives rise to fibroblasts in the meninges.
source: Furthermore, at E9.5, we detected Tbx18 expression in the vicinity of the neural tube, in a layer of MPs that gives rise to fibroblasts in the meninges (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), consistent with a previous report (DeSisto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: At E11.5, Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells were observed lining the ventral root and the spinal nerve with some of them closely attached to nerves in Tbx18Cre-ERT2 fate mapping experiments.
source: Tamoxifen was administrated to pregnant females at E9.5 and embryos were analyzed at E11.5 and E14.5. At E11.5, we observed Tom-positive/Sox10-negative cells lining the ventral root and the spinal nerve with some of them closely attached to nerves (Figure 4G–L).
evidence: This is shown by immunolabeling in Figure 4G–L.

claim: At E14.5, numerous Tom-positive cells were observed along blood vessels co-expressing NG2 or/and SMA in Tbx18Cre-ERT2 fate mapping experiments.
source: At E14.5, we observed numerous Tom-positive cells along blood vessels co-expressing NG2 or/and SMA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F, J–L).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F, J–L.

claim: Tom-positive cells along blood vessels at E14.5 in Tbx18Cre-ERT2 fate mapping experiments do not express Sox10.
source: At E14.5, we observed numerous Tom-positive cells along blood vessels co-expressing NG2 or/and SMA (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–F, J–L). None of them express Sox10 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–I, M–O).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G–I, M–O.

claim: Ventral root BCs expressing Egr2 have a dual embryonic origin: part of this population originates from the NC, while another may originate from the pial cells.
source: Together our observations suggest a dual embryonic origin of ventral root BCs expressing Egr2: part of this population originate from the NC, while another may originate from the pial cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Tbx18 lineage tracing and the absence of NC/neural tube contribution to MCs.

claim: Pial-derived cells, once in contact with the ventral root, activate Egr2, do not express Sox10, and then undergo migration along the nerves to the skin and mature into perivascular derivatives.
source: These latter population, once in contact with the ventral root, activate Egr2, do not express Sox10, and then undergo migration along the nerves to the skin and maturate into perivascular derivatives.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the integration of multiple observations.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis was performed on Tom-positive cells isolated by FACS from dissociated skin at E12.5.
source: To further characterize the molecular identity and the fate of their derivatives, we performed a single-cell transcriptomic analysis (single-cell RNA sequencing [scRNA-seq]) of traced Egr2-positive cells. As the quantification of traced cells in contact with nerves or blood vessels indicated that detachment was initiated at E12.5 (Figure 1M), we focused on this stage, on Tom-positive cells isolated by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) from dissociated skin.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for scRNA-seq.

claim: 2209 single-cell transcriptomes were analyzed with a mean number of expressed genes per cell of 5424 (SD 1491).
source: Using a customized pipeline (Materials and methods), we were able to analyze 2209 single-cell transcriptomes with a mean number of expressed genes per cell of 5424 (SD 1491).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the scRNA-seq dataset.

claim: No Cre expression was observed in the scRNA-seq analysis of Tom-positive cells.
source: As indicated above, to ensure that tomato expression was not due to ectopic Cre expression, we inserted the Cre sequence in our scRNA-seq analysis. We did not observe any Cre expression.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: 10 cell clusters were identified based on their expression patterns using the Seurat software.
source: Using the Seurat software (Stuart et al., 2019), we identified 10-cell clusters, based on their expression patterns (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result of computational analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The initial clusters were regrouped into three main cell type-defined supra-clusters: an SCP supra-cluster, a mesenchymal progenitor (MP) supra-cluster, and a smaller, isolated MC cluster.
source: This approach allowed us to regroup the initial clusters into three main cell type-defined supra-clusters: an SCP supra-cluster, a mesenchymal progenitor (MP) supra-cluster, and a smaller, isolated MC cluster (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result of the cluster analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The SCP supra-cluster contained 1031 cells (47%) that expressed high levels of SCP markers, such as Sox10, Erbb3, Fabp7, Plp1, Ngfr, and Cdh19.
source: The SCP supra-cluster contained 1031 cells (47%) that expressed high levels of SCP markers, such as Sox10, Erbb3, Fabp7, Plp1, Ngfr, and Cdh19 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative and qualitative description of the SCP cluster shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The MP supra-cluster contained 1056 cells (48%) that expressed a combination of mesenchymal markers, such as Pdgfra, Pdgfrb, Dlk1, Tbx18, Igf1, and Col1a1.
source: The MP supra-cluster contained 1056 cells (48%) that expressed a combination of mesenchymal markers, such as Pdgfra, Pdgfrb, Dlk1, Tbx18, Igf1, and Col1a1 (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative and qualitative description of the MP cluster shown in Figure 5C.

claim: 54% of traced cells at E12.5 showed either low or undetectable levels of expression of glial markers, such as Sox10, and significant expression of mesenchymal markers.
source: Interestingly, whereas most traced cells (90%) were in contact with nerves at E12.5 (Figure 1G and M), 54% of them showed either low or undetectable levels of expression of glial markers, such as Sox10, and significant expression of mesenchymal markers (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The isolated MC cluster contained 122 cells (6%) that expressed high levels of Pdgfrβ, Abcc9, Acta2, Cspg4, and Rgs5.
source: Finally, the isolated MC cluster contained 122 cells (6%) that expressed high levels of Pdgfrβ, Abcc9, Acta2, Cspg4, and Rgs5 (Figure 5C and D), which collectively constitute a signature for pericytes and vSMCs.
evidence: This is a quantitative and qualitative description of the MC cluster shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: The percentage of cells in the MC cluster (6%) is similar to the proportion of traced cells attached to blood vessels at E12.5.
source: This percentage is similar to the proportion of traced cells attached to blood vessels at E12.5 (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is a comparison between scRNA-seq data and quantification from immunohistochemistry.

claim: The cells in the MC cluster may have achieved their maturation into MCs.
source: Therefore, the latter cells may have achieved their maturation into MCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of mature MC markers.

claim: Further analyses using additional markers revealed a significant heterogeneity within the supra-clusters.
source: Further analyses using additional markers revealed a significant heterogeneity within the supra-clusters, in line with the identification of the 12 original clusters (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown by the expression patterns in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The SCP supra-cluster regroups four clusters (SCP1–4) that differ in the expression of SCP markers, such as Gap43, Pou3f1, and Pax3.
source: Hence, the SCP supra-cluster regroups four clusters (SCP1–4) that differ in the expression of SCP markers, such as Gap43, Pou3f1, and Pax3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The MP supra-cluster regroups five clusters: four of them (MP1–4) differentially express some MC progenitor genes, including Tbx18, Pax9, Kcnj8, or Acta2.
source: Similarly, the MP supra-cluster regroups five clusters: four of them (MP1–4) differentially express some MC progenitor genes, including Tbx18, Pax9, Kcnj8, or Acta2 (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereas MP5 displays a transcriptomic signature of chondroprogenitors with markers such as Sox9, Dlx5, Col2a1, and Fgfr2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C, D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MP5 displays a transcriptomic signature of chondroprogenitors with markers such as Sox9, Dlx5, Col2a1, and Fgfr2.
source: Similarly, the MP supra-cluster regroups five clusters: four of them (MP1–4) differentially express some MC progenitor genes, including Tbx18, Pax9, Kcnj8, or Acta2 (Figure 5C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), whereas MP5 displays a transcriptomic signature of chondroprogenitors with markers such as Sox9, Dlx5, Col2a1, and Fgfr2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In addition to mural progenitors, Egr2-positive BC cells may contribute to chondroprogenitors in the trunk.
source: These results suggest that in addition to mural progenitors, Egr2-positive BC cells may contribute to chondroprogenitors in the trunk.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the identification of the MP5 cluster with chondroprogenitor markers.

claim: The single-cell RNA analysis corroborates and extends the immunolabeling data.
source: In conclusion, the single-cell RNA analysis corroborates and extends the immunolabeling data presented above, and establish that Egr2-positive BC cells consist of two major subpopulations: a first one which evolves into SCP and is likely to derive from the NC, and a second one, which gives rise to derivatives with an MC identity and may originate from the mesenchymal precursors of meningeal fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion integrating scRNA-seq and immunolabeling data.

claim: Egr2-positive BC cells consist of two major subpopulations: a first one which evolves into SCP and is likely to derive from the NC, and a second one, which gives rise to derivatives with an MC identity and may originate from the mesenchymal precursors of meningeal fibroblasts.
source: In conclusion, the single-cell RNA analysis corroborates and extends the immunolabeling data presented above, and establish that Egr2-positive BC cells consist of two major subpopulations: a first one which evolves into SCP and is likely to derive from the NC, and a second one, which gives rise to derivatives with an MC identity and may originate from the mesenchymal precursors of meningeal fibroblasts.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including scRNA-seq, immunolabeling, and lineage tracing.

claim: Tom-positive cells without nerve contact were observed near the ventral roots at E11.5 in Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos.
source: As indicated above, in Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos, we observed Tom-positive cells without nerve contact, near the ventral roots at E11.5 and at the level of the developing pulmonary artery at E12.5 (Figure 1A and B, arrows).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 1A and B with arrows.

claim: Tom-positive cells without nerve contact were observed at the level of the developing pulmonary artery at E12.5 in Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos.
source: As indicated above, in Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom embryos, we observed Tom-positive cells without nerve contact, near the ventral roots at E11.5 and at the level of the developing pulmonary artery at E12.5 (Figure 1A and B, arrows).
evidence: This observation is shown in Figure 1B with arrows.

claim: Numerous Tom-positive MCs were found in the serous membranes (pre-tracheal fasciae, pericardium, and peritoneum) of adult Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom mice.
source: We performed a detailed study of two adult Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom mice and analyzed various organs (thyroid gland, lungs, heart, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, spleen, and kidneys) and serous membranes (pre-tracheal fasciae, pericardium, and peritoneum). Whereas we did not observe traced MCs in these organs, we found numerous Tom-positive MCs in the serous membranes that ensheath some of them, as revealed by co-labeling with PECAM of NG2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: No traced MCs were observed in various organs (thyroid gland, lungs, heart, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, spleen, and kidneys) of adult Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom mice.
source: We performed a detailed study of two adult Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom mice and analyzed various organs (thyroid gland, lungs, heart, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver, spleen, and kidneys) and serous membranes (pre-tracheal fasciae, pericardium, and peritoneum). Whereas we did not observe traced MCs in these organs, we found numerous Tom-positive MCs in the serous membranes that ensheath some of them, as revealed by co-labeling with PECAM of NG2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the analysis of adult mice.

claim: Tom-positive MCs in serous membranes do not form a continuum and are separated by non-traced MCs, suggesting at least another embryonic origin for MCs in serous membranes.
source: As described in the skin, Tom-positive MCs do not form a continuum and are separated by non-traced MCs, suggesting at least another embryonic origin for MCs in serous membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of traced and non-traced MCs.

claim: Serous membrane MCs derive from Egr2-expressing cells.
source: While these latter data demonstrate that serous membrane MCs derive from Egr2-expressing cells, in the absence of additional data on earlier Egr2 expression, it remains to be established whether they actually originate from BC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lineage tracing data.

claim: It remains to be established whether serous membrane MCs actually originate from BC cells.
source: While these latter data demonstrate that serous membrane MCs derive from Egr2-expressing cells, in the absence of additional data on earlier Egr2 expression, it remains to be established whether they actually originate from BC cells.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the current data.

claim: BC cells would provide a widespread contribution to the adult vasculature.
source: Nevertheless, the latter hypothesis is attractive, considering the precedent of the skin and the presence of such cells at the level of the pulmonary artery at E12.5. In this situation, BC cells would provide a widespread contribution to the adult vasculature.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the observations in skin and serous membranes.

claim: Genetic ablation of Egr2-expressing BC cells induced embryonic lethality at around E15.5.
source: We noticed that genetic ablation of Egr2-expressing cells induced embryonic lethality at around E15.5, as we were unable to obtain mutant embryos beyond that stage, and we often observed sites of necrosis in the uterus when collecting embryos at E15.5.
evidence: This is an observation from the genetic ablation experiments.

claim: Among 60 collected embryos from Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom × Egr2GFP(DT) breeding at E15.5, 10 were Egr2Cre/GFP(DT),Rosa26RTom based on PCR genotyping.
source: At E15.5, among the 60 collected embryos, issued from Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom × Egr2GFP(DT) breeding, 10 were Egr2Cre/GFP(DT),Rosa26RTom based on PCR genotyping.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the breeding experiment.

claim: Six out of 10 Egr2Cre/GFP(DT),Rosa26RTom embryos displayed traced cells in the skin, suggesting that BC cell ablation was not complete.
source: We analyzed these embryos for tomato fluorescence using a stereomicroscope. Unexpectedly, we observed traced cells in the skin in six of these embryos, suggesting that BC cell ablation was not complete.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of mutant embryos.

claim: Four Egr2Cre/GFP(DT),Rosa26RTom embryos displayed a complete loss of traced cells.
source: The four others displayed a complete loss of traced cells and were used for further analyses of the vascular network.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of mutant embryos.

claim: The skin vascular network appeared grossly similar in both mutant and control embryos at E15.5, with a dense network of arterioles, venules, and capillaries.
source: The skin vascular network appeared grossly similar in both types of embryos, with a dense network of arterioles, venules, and capillaries (Figure 6A–C, E, and G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A–C, E, and G.

claim: A significant reduction in the fraction of the vascular area covered by NG2-positive MCs was observed in the mutants (6.5%, SD 4.3%), as compared to the controls (17.9%, SD 2.0%).
source: However, when we compared the fraction of the vascular area covered by NG2-positive MCs (Figure 6D, F, and H), we observed a significant reduction in the mutants (6.5%, SD 4.3%), as compared to the controls (17.9%, SD 2.0%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement shown in Figure 6H.

claim: There was no significant difference between littermate controls and mutants in terms of Tuj1-positive area fraction and Sox10-positive cell count at E15.5.
source: We also explored whether Egr2-expressing cell ablation impacted nerve development and performed skin whole-mount immunohistochemistry for nerves (Tuj1) and SCPs (Sox10) at E15.5 in two controls and two mutants with complete loss of traced cells. There was no significant difference between littermate controls (Egr2Cre/+,Rosa26RTom) and mutants in terms of Tuj1-positive area fraction and Sox10-positive cell count (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The targeted ablation of Egr2-expressing cells does not appear to impact nerve development.
source: In conclusion, we find that the targeted ablation of Egr2-expressing cells does not appear to impact nerve development, but leads to a significant depletion of NG2-positive MCs in developing capillaries in the skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of nerve markers in mutants.

claim: The targeted ablation of Egr2-expressing cells leads to a significant depletion of NG2-positive MCs in developing capillaries in the skin.
source: In conclusion, we find that the targeted ablation of Egr2-expressing cells does not appear to impact nerve development, but leads to a significant depletion of NG2-positive MCs in developing capillaries in the skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantification of NG2-positive MCs in mutants.

claim: MCs from myeloid origin cannot fully compensate the defect caused by ablation of Egr2-expressing cells.
source: This indicates that MCs from myeloid origin cannot fully compensate this defect.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistent MC depletion in mutants.

claim: It remains to be determined whether the vascular phenotype is at the origin of embryonic lethality in Egr2 ablation mutants.
source: It remains to be determined whether this vascular phenotype is at the origin of embryonic lethality, as ablation targets all Egr2-positive cells and is therefore not limited to BC cells.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in interpreting the cause of lethality.

claim: About two thirds of newborn skin MCs originate from Egr2-expressing BC cells.
source: As about two thirds of newborn skin MCs originate from Egr2-expressing BC cells (Figure 3F and G), we questioned the functional importance of this population in blood vessel development.
evidence: This is based on the quantification data presented earlier (Figure 2E–G, not Figure 3F and G as stated).

claim: Approximately one third of the MC population in mouse skin derives from myeloid precursors.
source: This study uncovers a dual embryonic origin for MCs in mouse skin: while approximately one third of this population derives from myeloid precursors (Yamazaki et al., 2017), about two thirds originate from BCs.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work and the current quantification data.

claim: About two thirds of MCs in mouse skin originate from BCs.
source: This study uncovers a dual embryonic origin for MCs in mouse skin: while approximately one third of this population derives from myeloid precursors (Yamazaki et al., 2017), about two thirds originate from BCs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on quantification data.

claim: A specific subpopulation derived from Egr2-expressing, ventral BCs migrates along nerves into the skin, then detaches and gives rise to pericytes and vSMCs.
source: Hence, we identified a specific subpopulation derived from Egr2-expressing, ventral BCs that migrate along nerves into the skin, then detach and give rise to pericytes and vSMCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings of the study.

claim: The remaining BC-derived cells follow the same path as the MC-producing subpopulation, but remain attached to nerves and give birth to SCPs.
source: The remaining BC-derived cells follow the same path, but remain attached to nerves and give birth to SCPs.
evidence: This is a summary of findings distinguishing two BC-derived populations.

claim: BC-derived cells that remain attached to nerves and give birth to SCPs express the typical NC lineage marker Sox10.
source: Whereas these latter cells express the typical NC lineage marker Sox10, our observations suggest that the former population giving rise to MCs do not express this marker and originates from the developing pia matter.
evidence: This is based on the immunolabeling and scRNA-seq data showing Sox10 expression in SCP-fated cells.

claim: The BC-derived population giving rise to MCs does not express Sox10 and originates from the developing pia matter.
source: Whereas these latter cells express the typical NC lineage marker Sox10, our observations suggest that the former population giving rise to MCs do not express this marker and originates from the developing pia matter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of Sox10 expression and Tbx18 lineage tracing.

claim: Genetic ablation of Egr2-expressing BC cells results in a depletion of the skin MC compartment.
source: In accordance with our tracing studies, genetic ablation of Egr2-expressing BC cells results in a depletion of the skin MC compartment.
evidence: This is based on the quantification of NG2-positive MCs in ablation mutants.

claim: Numerous MCs in serous membranes protecting the trachea, heart, and digestive tract are derived from Egr2-expressing cells.
source: Finally, we found that numerous MCs in serous membranes protecting the trachea, heart, and digestive tract are derived from Egr2-expressing cells, suggesting a broader implication of BCs in the development of the systemic vasculature.
evidence: This is based on the lineage tracing data in adult serous membranes.

claim: BCs have a broader implication in the development of the systemic vasculature.
source: Finally, we found that numerous MCs in serous membranes protecting the trachea, heart, and digestive tract are derived from Egr2-expressing cells, suggesting a broader implication of BCs in the development of the systemic vasculature.
evidence: This is a suggestion based on the widespread distribution of Egr2-traced MCs.

claim: The observations highlight a novel role for BCs in peripheral vascular development.
source: Our observations highlight a novel role for BCs in peripheral vascular development and further expand peripheral glia recently reported broad potential (Adameyko et al., 2009; Dyachuk et al., 2014; Espinosa-Medina et al., 2014; Furlan et al., 2017; Kaucka et al., 2016; Uesaka et al., 2015; Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a summary statement placing the findings in the context of previous work on glial cell plasticity.

claim: Virtually all BC cells at the dorsal root express Sox10 and give rise to either SCP or DRG sensory neurons.
source: While virtually all BC cells at the dorsal root express Sox10 and give rise to either SCP or DRG sensory neurons, the situation appears more complex in the ventral roots.
evidence: This is stated as an established observation from the current and previous studies.

claim: Ventral roots encompass two populations of Egr2-expressing BCs with distinct molecular and functional profiles.
source: We discovered that ventral roots encompass two populations of Egr2-expressing BCs with distinct molecular and functional profiles.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the molecular and fate mapping data.

claim: In addition to the Sox10-positive BCs at the origin of SCPs that migrate along nerve roots and spinal nerves, there is a population of Sox10-negative BC-derived cells that express mesenchymal markers such as Tbx18, Col1a1, and Pdgfra.
source: In addition to the Sox10-positive BCs at the origin of SCPs that migrate along nerve roots and spinal nerves, we identified a population of Sox10-negative BC-derived cells that express mesenchymal markers such as Tbx18, Col1a1, and Pdgfra.
evidence: This is based on the immunolabeling and RNAscope data showing these markers in Tom-positive cells.

claim: The scRNA-seq analysis of traced cells extracted from E12.5 skin supports the presence of nerve-attached BC derivatives with mesenchymal signature.
source: Our scRNA-seq analysis of traced cells extracted from E12.5 skin, at a time when the majority of BC-derived cells are still in contact with nerves, further supports the presence of nerve-attached BC derivatives with mesenchymal signature.
evidence: This is based on the identification of the MP supra-cluster in the scRNA-seq data.

claim: At E12.5, myeloid precursors are recruited by the primitive vascular plexus to form MCs.
source: Interestingly, at the same time, myeloid precursors are recruited by the primitive vascular plexus to form MCs (Yamazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: In both BC-derived and myeloid-derived MC systems, traced cells along blood vessels do not form continuous blocks, but are interrupted by blocks of non-traced cells.
source: In both systems, traced cells along blood vessels do not form continuous blocks, but are interrupted by blocks of non-traced cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the lineage tracing data.

claim: There exists an attraction mechanism operated by the developing vascular plexus and acting on neighboring cell populations of at least two distinct origins, which have the potential to mature into MCs.
source: This suggests the existence of an attraction mechanism operated by the developing vascular plexus and acting on neighboring cell populations of at least two distinct origins, which have the potential to mature into MCs.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed to explain the pattern of MC recruitment.

claim: Nerves act as a track for the migration of BC-derived MCs from the ventral BCs to the skin and probably some deeper structures in the developing embryo.
source: In this scenario, nerves would act as a track for the migration of one of these populations from the ventral BCs to the skin and probably some deeper structures in the developing embryo.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed migration pattern.

claim: The migration of BC derivatives along all spinal nerves is likely to provide an important source of MCs to the developing embryonic skin.
source: Since this migration of BC derivatives was observed along all spinal nerves, this mechanism is likely to provide an important source of MCs to the developing embryonic skin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the widespread distribution of the migration pattern.

claim: Egr2 inactivation does not appear to have any obvious effect on the migration and differentiation of BC-derived MCs.
source: Notably, Egr2 inactivation does not appear to have any obvious effect on the migration and differentiation of this population.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of mutant and control embryos.

claim: More detailed analyses will be required to exclude any later function of Egr2 in MCs.
source: Nevertheless, more detailed analyses will be required to exclude any later function in MCs.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in the current analysis.

claim: The common derivatives observed in Egr2 and Prss56 tracing studies are likely to reflect an already noticed, partial overlap between Prss56- and Egr2-positive BC subpopulations.
source: The common derivatives observed in the two tracing studies are likely to reflect an already noticed, partial overlap between Prss56- and Egr2-positive BC subpopulations (Gresset et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison with previous work.

claim: The differences in fates observed in the skin between Egr2 and Prss56 tracing point to the existence of a functional heterogeneity within BC cells.
source: In contrast, the differences in fates observed in the skin points to the existence of a functional heterogeneity within BC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the different derivatives observed with different markers.

claim: The studies support an early specification in the development of ventral BC cells.
source: Our studies support such an early specification in the development of ventral BC cells; genetic tracing of cells expressing Tbx18 indicate that some of them attach to ventral roots before E11.5, where they do not express Sox10 and may activate Egr2.
evidence: This is based on the Tbx18 lineage tracing showing early attachment to ventral roots.

claim: Genetic tracing of cells expressing Tbx18 indicates that some of them attach to ventral roots before E11.5, where they do not express Sox10 and may activate Egr2.
source: Our studies support such an early specification in the development of ventral BC cells; genetic tracing of cells expressing Tbx18 indicate that some of them attach to ventral roots before E11.5, where they do not express Sox10 and may activate Egr2.
evidence: This is based on the Tbx18 lineage tracing data.

claim: Tbx18-traced cells likely contribute to the Egr2-traced subpopulation that migrates along nerves to the skin, detaches and differentiates into MCs.
source: It is likely that these cells contribute to the Egr2-traced subpopulation that migrates along nerves to the skin, detaches and differentiates into MCs.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the Tbx18 lineage to the MC-producing population.

claim: The findings require revisiting the simplistic concept of BCs as transient and homogenous clusters of stem-like cells.
source: In accordance, our findings require to revisit the simplistic concept of BCs as transient and homogenous clusters of stem-like cells, characterized by co-expression of a panel of markers including Egr2 and Prss56 and initially thought to be entirely derived from the NC.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion based on the demonstration of BC heterogeneity.

claim: Ventral exit point BCs possess mixed NC and mesenchymal origins.
source: The present data suggest that ventral exit point BCs possess mixed NC and mesenchymal origins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lineage tracing data showing contributions from both NC and Tbx18-expressing cells.

claim: The Egr2-expressing BC cells that give rise to MCs are neither derived from the NC nor from the neural tube.
source: In particular, we show that the Egr2-expressing BC cells that give rise to MCs are neither derived from the NC nor from the neural tube.
evidence: This is based on the negative results from Wnt1Cre, Sox10Cre-Ert2, and Olig2Cre lineage tracing.

claim: The Egr2-expressing BC cells that give rise to MCs are likely to originate from Tbx18-expressing cells that are also at the origin of developing meningeal fibroblasts.
source: They are likely to originate from Tbx18-expressing cells that are also at the origin of developing meningeal fibroblasts (DeSisto et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on the Tbx18 lineage tracing and citation to previous work on meningeal fibroblast origins.

claim: Molecular heterogeneity was observed within NC-derived BCs, as they contain populations expressing either Egr2 or Prss56, or co-expressing both markers.
source: Actually, molecular heterogeneity was also observed within NC-derived BCs, as they contain populations expressing either Egr2 or Prss56, or co-expressing both markers (Gresset et al., 2015 and unpublished results).
evidence: This is based on published and unpublished observations.

claim: Heterogeneity in the embryonic origin of BC cells is likely to explain why targeted ablation of NC-derived cells expressing Egr2 is effective but not lethal before birth, whereas targeted ablation of all Egr2-expressing cells leads to embryonic death at around E15.5.
source: This heterogeneity in the embryonic origin of BC cells is likely to explain another observation: whereas targeted ablation of NC-derived cells expressing Egr2, obtained by combining Wnt1Cre and Egr2GFP/DT alleles, is effective, but not lethal before birth (Odelin et al., 2018), targeted ablation of all Egr2-expressing cells does lead to embryonic death at around E15.5 (this study).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the heterogeneity to the differential lethality phenotypes.

claim: Targeted ablation of NC-derived cells expressing Egr2, obtained by combining Wnt1Cre and Egr2GFP/DT alleles, is effective, but not lethal before birth.
source: This heterogeneity in the embryonic origin of BC cells is likely to explain another observation: whereas targeted ablation of NC-derived cells expressing Egr2, obtained by combining Wnt1Cre and Egr2GFP/DT alleles, is effective, but not lethal before birth (Odelin et al., 2018), targeted ablation of all Egr2-expressing cells does lead to embryonic death at around E15.5 (this study).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The populations ablated in NC-specific versus pan-Egr2 ablation experiments do not completely overlap.
source: This may be explained by the fact that the populations ablated in those experiments do not completely overlap.
evidence: This is an inference explaining the differential lethality.

claim: MCs have been divided into pericytes that ensheath capillaries, and vSMCs that cover arterioles, venules, and larger vessels based on their location.
source: Based on their location, MCs have been divided into pericytes that ensheath capillaries, and vSMCs that cover arterioles, venules, and larger vessels (Armulik et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: The simplistic view of MCs has been recently challenged by growing evidence supporting a continuum of MC lineages with intermediate types associated to specific functions.
source: However, this simplistic view has been recently challenged by growing evidence supporting a continuum of MC lineages with intermediate types associated to specific functions (Holm et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to recent literature.

claim: Molecular analysis of CNS MCs at the single-cell level revealed the existence of subpopulations specifically involved in processes such as inflammation.
source: For instance, molecular analysis of CNS MCs at the single-cell level revealed the existence of subpopulations specifically involved in processes such as inflammation (Duan et al., 2018) or fibrosis (Göritz et al., 2011; Soderblom et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Molecular analysis of CNS MCs at the single-cell level revealed the existence of subpopulations specifically involved in fibrosis.
source: For instance, molecular analysis of CNS MCs at the single-cell level revealed the existence of subpopulations specifically involved in processes such as inflammation (Duan et al., 2018) or fibrosis (Göritz et al., 2011; Soderblom et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated based on citations to previous studies.

claim: A similar heterogeneity among NG2-positive MCs has recently been reported in the skin, with different subpopulations at specific locations and with differing roles in wound repair.
source: A similar heterogeneity among NG2-positive MCs has recently been reported in the skin, with different subpopulations at specific locations and with differing roles in wound repair (Goss et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to recent work.

claim: The study reveals the existence of at least two embryonic origins for both skin pericytes and vSMCs, BC derivatives and myeloid precursors, which are recruited during the same period to form MCs.
source: Our study reveals the existence of at least two embryonic origins for both skin pericytes and vSMCs, BCs derivatives and myeloid precursors, which are recruited during the same period to form MCs.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings.

claim: Each MC population (BC-derived and myeloid-derived) appears to be unable to fully compensate the other upon depletion.
source: Each population appears to be unable to fully compensate the other upon depletion: we report that targeted ablation of BC cells results in a significant decrease in NG2-positive MCs at E15.5 and, conversely, Yamazaki and colleagues have shown that in PU.1 (also known as Spi1) mutants, depleted of tissue myeloid cells, there is also a loss of MCs at E15.5 (Yamazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the current ablation data and citation to previous work on myeloid cell depletion.

claim: Targeted ablation of BC cells results in a significant decrease in NG2-positive MCs at E15.5.
source: Each population appears to be unable to fully compensate the other upon depletion: we report that targeted ablation of BC cells results in a significant decrease in NG2-positive MCs at E15.5 and, conversely, Yamazaki and colleagues have shown that in PU.1 (also known as Spi1) mutants, depleted of tissue myeloid cells, there is also a loss of MCs at E15.5 (Yamazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on the quantification data from the ablation experiments.

claim: In PU.1 mutants, depleted of tissue myeloid cells, there is a loss of MCs at E15.5.
source: Each population appears to be unable to fully compensate the other upon depletion: we report that targeted ablation of BC cells results in a significant decrease in NG2-positive MCs at E15.5 and, conversely, Yamazaki and colleagues have shown that in PU.1 (also known as Spi1) mutants, depleted of tissue myeloid cells, there is also a loss of MCs at E15.5 (Yamazaki et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated based on citation to previous work.

claim: The data show molecular differences between MP clusters susceptible to give rise to MCs in the peripheral vasculature.
source: In addition, our data show molecular differences between MP clusters susceptible to give rise to MCs in the peripheral vasculature, with most MP clusters (1–4) sharing molecular markers (Pdgfrα and Col1a1) with CNS MC subtypes involved in fibrosis.
evidence: This is based on the scRNA-seq analysis showing different marker expression in MP clusters.

claim: Most MP clusters (1–4) share molecular markers (Pdgfrα and Col1a1) with CNS MC subtypes involved in fibrosis.
source: In addition, our data show molecular differences between MP clusters susceptible to give rise to MCs in the peripheral vasculature, with most MP clusters (1–4) sharing molecular markers (Pdgfrα and Col1a1) with CNS MC subtypes involved in fibrosis.
evidence: This is based on comparison of marker expression between the current data and previous CNS MC studies.

claim: Whether differences in embryonic origin or marker expression identify distinct functional lineages corresponding to those reported at later stages remains an open question.
source: Whether these differences in embryonic origin or marker expression identify distinct functional lineages corresponding to those reported at later stages remains an open question.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation and future direction.
